hypothesis: If the claim holds, the measured surface of a resting biconcave mammalian red blood cell has non-constant mean curvature (the membrane does not satisfy the Young-Laplace condition for a pure surface-tension interface), and the cell becomes spherical when the suspending medium is hypotonic.
pass_criterion: In at least 90% of resting discocytes with 3D surface reconstructions, the coefficient of variation of the mean curvature H over the surface (excluding the rim singularity) is above 0.5 and the sign of H changes between the dimple and the rim. In addition, cells in hypotonic medium (at or below about 150 mOsm/kg) must show sphericity above 0.9.
fail_criterion: In more than 50% of resting discocytes, H is constant within measurement error (coefficient of variation below 0.15, no sign change). The claim is also refuted if the discocyte shape is not lost, or the cell does not become spherical, in hypotonic medium.
interpretation: Thompson's 'surface of equilibrium' for surface tension alone is a constant-mean-curvature surface, since the pressure difference across a fluid-fluid interface is 2*gamma*H. His 'fluid drop suspended in another liquid' maps to a closed surface with uniform H. Modern reinterpretation: the shape is held by the spectrin-actin cytoskeleton, membrane bending elasticity (Helfrich) and the area-to-volume ratio, not by tension alone. So a measured non-constant H is consistent with his 'some other force' but not with his specific guesses (osmotic inequilibrium, cholesterin fluid crystals). The test covers only the negative claim (not a CMC surface) and the shape change to a sphere in dilute medium. It does not cover his candidate mechanisms.
no_dataset_reason: I could not confirm any specific public dataset of 3D red-cell surface reconstructions, with matched hypotonic and isotonic conditions, that has a landing page and DOI I am sure resolves. Candidates I recall include holotomography and quantitative phase imaging data, the Chula RBC-12 image set and Broad Bioimage Benchmark Collection images. I could not verify their URLs or DOIs, and 2D smear images cannot give mean curvature. Naming an unverified identifier would risk a fabricated citation, so I report null. The test could be run if a verified deposit of 3D RBC tomograms (Zenodo or figshare) is later identified.
